sourceNote: Senior full-stack interview master bank for a 7-year developer. Main questions are conventional interview questions, grouped only into Simple, Medium and Complex. Every question has a clear interview answer, a concrete real-world engineering example, deeper reasoning, senior-level considerations, common mistakes and concept-specific follow-ups. Scenario-based questions remain separate.

questions.question: What is the difference between a class and a struct in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: A class is a reference type; a struct is a value type. I choose based on semantics first: an Order has identity and is normally a class, while a small immutable Money or Coordinate can be a struct.
questions.detailedAnswer: The key differences are copying, identity, nullability, inheritance rules and boxing. Large or mutable structs can be expensive and confusing because assignments copy the value. Structs are strongest for small value-like data.
questions.example: For an Order service, two variables can refer to the same Order object, so changing the object is visible through both references. A small readonly Money value can be copied safely. I would not choose a struct just to avoid allocations without measuring.
questions.seniorPerspective: A senior answer connects the language rule to domain semantics and performance evidence rather than saying structs are always faster.
questions.commonMistakes: Using a struct only because it is a value type; creating large mutable structs; ignoring boxing and copying.
followUps: Can a struct be null?
What happens when a struct is boxed?
When would readonly struct help?

questions.question: What is the difference between interface and abstract class in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: An interface defines a contract that unrelated types can implement; an abstract class can provide shared state and implementation. I prefer interfaces for replaceable dependencies and abstract classes only when there is real shared behavior.
questions.detailedAnswer: Interfaces support multiple implementations and keep dependencies loosely coupled. Abstract classes are useful when common implementation is part of the design, but they create stronger inheritance coupling.
questions.example: A checkout service can depend on IPaymentGateway while StripeGateway and BankGateway implement it. An abstract base class makes sense when several gateways genuinely share protected workflow logic and invariants.
questions.seniorPerspective: The important senior decision is whether the abstraction represents a capability or a shared implementation.
questions.commonMistakes: Creating interfaces for every class without a meaningful boundary; using inheritance just to reuse a few lines of code.
followUps: When would composition be better?
Can a class implement multiple interfaces?
How would you unit test the abstraction?

questions.question: What is the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable?
questions.shortAnswer: IEnumerable represents iteration over data already available to the application, while IQueryable can build an expression that a provider such as EF Core translates into a database query.
questions.detailedAnswer: The boundary is where execution happens. IQueryable is useful at a data-provider boundary; once materialized, subsequent LINQ runs in memory.
questions.example: If an orders table has millions of rows, filtering with IQueryable before ToListAsync lets SQL Server perform the filtering. Calling ToListAsync first and then filtering with LINQ to Objects moves the work into application memory.
questions.seniorPerspective: A senior developer watches generated SQL, result size and provider limitations instead of assuming every LINQ expression has the same cost.
questions.commonMistakes: Materializing too early; exposing IQueryable across unrelated layers without control; assuming every C# method can translate to SQL.
followUps: What happens with AsEnumerable?
How do you inspect generated SQL?
When would you intentionally materialize?

questions.question: What are async and await used for in C#?
questions.shortAnswer: They let an application start an asynchronous operation and continue without blocking a thread while I/O is pending. They improve scalability for I/O-bound work; they do not automatically make CPU work faster.
questions.detailedAnswer: Async is most valuable for I/O such as HTTP, database, files and messaging. CPU-heavy work needs a different strategy; wrapping synchronous CPU work in Task.Run inside a server request is not a universal performance fix.
questions.example: An API receives a request, calls SQL Server and another HTTP service, and awaits both. While the database or HTTP server is working, the ASP.NET Core thread can serve other requests.
questions.seniorPerspective: I look for end-to-end async flow and avoid blocking with Result or Wait, especially in server code.
questions.commonMistakes: Calling .Result or .Wait; using async void for normal application code; assuming async means parallel.
followUps: Does async create a new thread?
When would Task.WhenAll help?
What happens if one awaited operation fails?

questions.question: What are Transient, Scoped and Singleton lifetimes in ASP.NET Core dependency injection?
questions.shortAnswer: Transient creates a new instance each time requested, Scoped normally creates one per request scope, and Singleton keeps one instance for the application lifetime.
questions.detailedAnswer: The lifetime must match state ownership and thread-safety. A singleton must not capture a scoped dependency, and mutable singleton state needs synchronization or should be avoided.
questions.example: A DbContext is commonly scoped so one HTTP request can share its unit-of-work context. A stateless formatter can be transient. A thread-safe configuration or cache service can be singleton.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose a lifetime by ownership and concurrency semantics, not by habit.
questions.commonMistakes: Registering everything as singleton; injecting scoped services into singletons; storing request-specific state in singleton objects.
followUps: What is a captive dependency?
Is DbContext thread-safe?
When would you choose transient?

questions.question: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: Middleware is a component in the HTTP request pipeline that can inspect, modify, short-circuit or pass a request to the next component.
questions.detailedAnswer: Ordering matters because middleware wraps later components. Authentication must run before authorization, and short-circuiting middleware can prevent the endpoint from executing.
questions.example: A request can pass through exception handling, correlation ID, authentication, authorization and endpoint execution middleware. Exception handling should be early enough to observe failures from later middleware.
questions.seniorPerspective: I explain middleware as an ordered pipeline and discuss why the order changes behavior.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating middleware order as cosmetic; putting endpoint-specific logic into global middleware; exposing exception details to clients.
followUps: Middleware vs filters?
Where would global exception handling go?
How would you add correlation IDs?

questions.question: What is dependency injection and why is it useful?
questions.shortAnswer: Dependency injection supplies a class's dependencies from outside instead of making the class construct them itself. It reduces coupling and improves testing and replacement.
questions.detailedAnswer: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit. DI also centralizes lifecycle management and allows infrastructure implementations to change without rewriting business logic.
questions.example: OrderService can receive IOrderRepository and IClock through its constructor. A unit test can provide a fake repository and fixed clock without changing OrderService.
questions.seniorPerspective: The senior value is not the container itself; it is dependency direction and clear boundaries.
questions.commonMistakes: Injecting dozens of services into one class; hiding required dependencies in service locators; creating infrastructure objects directly inside business logic.
followUps: How do you detect a class with too many dependencies?
When is DI overkill?
How do lifetimes affect DI?

questions.question: What is the difference between a component and a service in Angular?
questions.shortAnswer: A component owns UI state and presentation behavior; a service encapsulates reusable application logic, data access or shared state.
questions.detailedAnswer: Components should stay focused on the view boundary. Services can be injected and tested independently, but a service should not become a dumping ground for unrelated behavior.
questions.example: A CustomerListComponent handles rendering and user events while CustomerService calls the API. Keeping HTTP code in the service prevents multiple components from duplicating request logic.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use boundaries that make responsibilities and testing obvious.
questions.commonMistakes: Putting all business logic in components; creating a giant shared service; using services as global mutable state without a reason.
followUps: Where should API calls live?
How would components share state?
When would you create a facade?

questions.question: What is the difference between an Observable and a Promise?
questions.shortAnswer: A Promise represents one eventual result, while an Observable represents a stream that can emit values over time and can be composed with RxJS operators.
questions.detailedAnswer: Observables support cancellation and stream composition, which is important for Angular event and HTTP flows. Promises are simpler when only one result matters.
questions.example: A login call may naturally return one result, while a search box can emit many terms. switchMap can cancel or ignore stale HTTP searches when a new term arrives.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose based on whether the problem is a one-shot result or a stream with composition and cancellation needs.
questions.commonMistakes: Subscribing everywhere without cleanup; nesting subscriptions; using an Observable just because Angular supports it.
followUps: What does switchMap do?
How do you avoid subscription leaks?
When is a Promise simpler?

questions.question: What is Angular change detection?
questions.shortAnswer: Change detection checks whether template-bound values need to be reflected in the DOM. Angular can reduce unnecessary work when components use OnPush and predictable state updates.
questions.detailedAnswer: The important point is not memorizing every internal step; it is controlling state changes and avoiding unnecessary work in large component trees.
questions.example: A dashboard with many widgets can avoid checking every subtree after unrelated events by using OnPush and immutable or signal-based state updates.
questions.seniorPerspective: I measure rendering cost before optimizing and keep component state flows explicit.
questions.commonMistakes: Mutating nested objects while expecting OnPush to notice every case; triggering excessive work from template functions; optimizing without profiling.
followUps: What is OnPush?
How do signals interact with change detection?
How would you debug a slow UI?

questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
questions.shortAnswer: A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its lexical scope even after the outer function has returned.
questions.detailedAnswer: Closures are useful for encapsulation and callbacks, but long-lived closures can retain references and contribute to memory leaks if attached to long-lived objects or subscriptions.
questions.example: A createRetryHandler function can keep a retry count private inside its closure. The returned function can update that count without exposing it globally.
questions.seniorPerspective: I think about both lexical behavior and object lifetime when using closures.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming the variables are copied rather than retained by reference; creating accidental long-lived references; confusing closure scope with this binding.
followUps: How does closure differ from this?
Can closures cause memory leaks?
Where have you used closures in UI code?

questions.question: What is the difference between let, const and var?
questions.shortAnswer: let and const are block-scoped; var is function-scoped. const prevents reassignment of the binding but does not make an object immutable.
questions.detailedAnswer: Modern TypeScript and JavaScript code normally prefer const by default, let when reassignment is required, and avoid var unless maintaining legacy code.
questions.example: Inside a loop that creates asynchronous callbacks, let gives each iteration its own block-scoped binding. A const configuration object can still have its properties changed unless the object is frozen.
questions.seniorPerspective: The important interview point is scope and mutation semantics, not simply saying const means immutable.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying const makes objects immutable; using var in new code without a reason; ignoring temporal dead zone behavior.
followUps: What is the temporal dead zone?
Is const object immutable?
How did let fix common loop bugs?

questions.question: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
questions.shortAnswer: INNER JOIN returns matching rows from both sides. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and adds matching right-side data when available.
questions.detailedAnswer: Join choice is driven by the business result set. A LEFT JOIN followed by a WHERE condition on the right table can accidentally behave like an INNER JOIN.
questions.example: To list all customers including those without orders, start with Customers LEFT JOIN Orders. An INNER JOIN would remove customers who have never placed an order.
questions.seniorPerspective: I verify the expected row cardinality with a small dataset before tuning the query.
questions.commonMistakes: Choosing joins by habit; filtering the right table in WHERE unintentionally; ignoring duplicate rows caused by one-to-many relationships.
followUps: How would you find customers with no orders?
Why can joins multiply rows?
When would EXISTS be better?

questions.question: What is an index and why does it improve query performance?
questions.shortAnswer: An index is an additional data structure that helps the database locate rows without scanning the whole table. It speeds some reads but adds storage and write cost.
questions.detailedAnswer: Indexes should follow actual predicates, joins and ordering patterns. Too many indexes increase insert and update cost and can still be ineffective when selectivity is poor.
questions.example: If an API frequently searches Orders by CustomerId and CreatedAt, a suitable composite index can reduce the rows SQL Server must examine.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design indexes from query patterns and verify them with execution plans and measured workload.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding an index to every column; ignoring write cost; assuming an index guarantees a seek.
followUps: What is a covering index?
What is a composite index order?
How do you validate an index change?

questions.question: What is a transaction?
questions.shortAnswer: A transaction groups related database changes so the database can enforce an atomic unit of work according to the chosen isolation level.
questions.detailedAnswer: Transactions protect consistency, but long transactions increase locking and contention. The correct boundary should be as small as possible while protecting the required invariant.
questions.example: When placing an order, inserting the order header and reserving inventory may need one transaction if the business invariant requires both to succeed together.
questions.seniorPerspective: I define the business invariant first, then choose the smallest transaction that guarantees it.
questions.commonMistakes: Opening transactions around slow external calls; assuming transactions solve distributed consistency; ignoring isolation and lock duration.
followUps: What are ACID properties?
What is isolation level?
How do you handle a transaction failure?

questions.question: What are the main components you consider when designing a backend service?
questions.shortAnswer: I start with clients, API boundaries, business logic, data stores, external dependencies, asynchronous messaging where needed, observability and security.
questions.detailedAnswer: The architecture should follow requirements such as scale, consistency, latency and failure tolerance rather than starting with a list of technologies.
questions.example: For an order API, I would define REST endpoints, an application layer, SQL storage, payment integration, an event mechanism for notifications, metrics, logs and authorization.
questions.seniorPerspective: Even a simple design should state assumptions and identify the critical failure paths.
questions.commonMistakes: Jumping directly to Kafka, microservices or Kubernetes; ignoring data ownership; forgetting observability and security.
followUps: How would the design change at 10x traffic?
Where would you cache?
What happens when the database is unavailable?

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.shortAnswer: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization determines what that authenticated identity is allowed to do.
questions.detailedAnswer: Authentication answers identity; authorization answers permission. Authorization must be enforced server-side for protected resources.
questions.example: A user may successfully sign in and receive a token, but an endpoint that edits another customer's account must still check whether that user has permission to perform the operation.
questions.seniorPerspective: I always separate identity verification from resource-level permission checks.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating a valid JWT as proof that every operation is allowed; relying only on Angular route guards; checking roles without resource ownership where needed.
followUps: What is RBAC?
What is IDOR?
Why can frontend authorization never be the only control?

questions.question: What is RAG and why is it useful?
questions.shortAnswer: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant approved information and supplies it to the model before generation, reducing dependence on model memory for changing or private knowledge.
questions.detailedAnswer: A production RAG pipeline needs chunking, metadata, retrieval quality, prompt construction, access control and evaluation; retrieval alone does not guarantee a correct answer.
questions.example: An internal support assistant can retrieve current product documentation and incident runbooks, then answer with source references. Updating the documents changes the knowledge without retraining the model.
questions.seniorPerspective: I would measure retrieval and answer quality separately and enforce document-level authorization.
questions.commonMistakes: Using a vector database as a substitute for authorization; retrieving too much context; evaluating only with a few demo questions.
followUps: How do you evaluate retrieval?
How do you prevent cross-tenant retrieval?
What should happen when no relevant document is found?

questions.question: What is the difference between Task.WhenAll and awaiting tasks sequentially?
questions.shortAnswer: Task.WhenAll allows independent asynchronous operations to progress concurrently; sequential awaits wait for one operation before starting the next if the tasks are created sequentially.
questions.detailedAnswer: Concurrency is appropriate only when operations are independent and downstream capacity can handle it. It does not make one database query inherently faster.
questions.example: A dashboard endpoint needs profile, notifications and preferences from independent services. Starting all three tasks and awaiting Task.WhenAll can reduce total latency toward the slowest call rather than the sum of all calls.
questions.seniorPerspective: I consider dependency relationships, cancellation, failure handling and downstream load before introducing concurrency.
questions.commonMistakes: Parallelizing dependent operations; firing hundreds of tasks without a limit; forgetting that one failure affects WhenAll completion.
followUps: How are exceptions handled?
How would you limit concurrency?
Can DbContext operations run in parallel?

questions.question: What is deferred execution in LINQ and why can it surprise developers?
questions.shortAnswer: Many LINQ operators build a query that executes when enumerated rather than when defined. This means the source can change or expensive work can run multiple times.
questions.detailedAnswer: Materialize deliberately when you need a stable snapshot or when repeated enumeration would be expensive. Keep provider-backed queries controlled so database work is explicit.
questions.example: If a filtered IQueryable is enumerated twice, it can issue two database queries. If an IEnumerable wraps a costly computation, repeated enumeration can repeat the computation.
questions.seniorPerspective: I watch execution boundaries and do not assume a LINQ variable contains data merely because the query expression was created.
questions.commonMistakes: Calling Count then ToList and accidentally executing two queries; enumerating expensive sequences repeatedly; hiding database calls behind properties.
followUps: When does ToList execute?
What happens with IQueryable?
How would you avoid repeated queries?

questions.question: How does exception handling affect API design?
questions.shortAnswer: Exceptions should represent unexpected or exceptional failures, while expected business outcomes can be modeled explicitly. API middleware should translate unhandled exceptions into consistent responses without leaking internals.
questions.detailedAnswer: A good design separates logging, client response mapping and domain behavior. Exceptions should retain diagnostic context while responses expose only appropriate information.
questions.example: An OrderService can return a domain result for an expected validation failure such as an unavailable product. An unexpected database outage can propagate to centralized exception handling, which logs correlation data and returns a safe 500 response.
questions.seniorPerspective: I want one consistent error contract, structured logs and clear ownership of where errors are handled.
questions.commonMistakes: Catching Exception everywhere; returning stack traces to clients; logging the same exception at every layer; using exceptions for normal control flow.
followUps: How would you map domain errors to HTTP status codes?
Where should logging happen?
How would you preserve correlation IDs?

questions.question: How does ASP.NET Core request cancellation work and why should services honor CancellationToken?
questions.shortAnswer: CancellationToken lets a request signal that work is no longer needed. Propagating it to database and HTTP operations can stop wasted work after a client disconnects or a timeout occurs.
questions.detailedAnswer: Cancellation is cooperative. Every layer must accept and pass the token to operations that support cancellation, while cleanup and partial work need explicit consideration.
questions.example: A report endpoint starts a long SQL query and the user closes the browser. Passing HttpContext.RequestAborted to EF Core allows the database operation to be cancelled where supported instead of continuing unnecessarily.
questions.seniorPerspective: I treat cancellation as resource management, not just an API parameter.
questions.commonMistakes: Accepting a token but never passing it onward; swallowing OperationCanceledException incorrectly; assuming cancellation instantly kills every operation.
followUps: Where should the token originate?
How does cancellation affect database calls?
Should cancellation be logged as an error?

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization middleware in ASP.NET Core?
questions.shortAnswer: Authentication establishes the ClaimsPrincipal from credentials such as a bearer token. Authorization evaluates policies or roles against that identity and the requested resource.
questions.detailedAnswer: Authentication must occur before authorization. Resource-based authorization can go beyond roles when access depends on ownership or business rules.
questions.example: A JWT bearer handler validates the token and creates the user principal. An authorization policy then requires the SupportAgent role or a specific claim before the controller executes.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design authorization around the protected resource, not only around endpoint roles.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming authentication means access is granted; putting authorization only in Angular; using roles for every resource rule.
followUps: How do policies work?
What is resource-based authorization?
What response should a forbidden request receive?

questions.question: How would you prevent an N+1 query problem in EF Core?
questions.shortAnswer: N+1 happens when one query loads a set and then triggers another query for each item. I prevent it with deliberate projection, appropriate eager loading or batched queries.
questions.detailedAnswer: The correct fix depends on the required data shape. Projection can reduce payload and tracking cost; Include is useful when the entity graph itself is needed.
questions.example: Instead of loading 500 orders and then querying Customer for each order, project the required customer name in one SQL query. For a read endpoint, Select into a DTO is often clearer than loading an entire object graph.
questions.seniorPerspective: I inspect generated SQL and query counts rather than relying on ORM intuition.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding Include everywhere; lazy loading without awareness; loading full entities when only three fields are needed.
followUps: How would you detect N+1 in production?
When is Include appropriate?
Why is projection often faster?

questions.question: How does switchMap help with search or autocomplete?
questions.shortAnswer: switchMap switches to the newest inner Observable and unsubscribes from the previous one. It is useful when only the latest user input matters.
questions.detailedAnswer: The operator expresses a business rule: only the latest request matters. For operations that must all complete, mergeMap or another operator may be appropriate.
questions.example: A user types 'ang', then 'angu'. The first HTTP search may still be in flight. switchMap ensures the current search replaces the previous stream so stale results do not overwrite the latest result.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose an RxJS flattening operator based on concurrency semantics, not by memorizing operator names.
questions.commonMistakes: Using mergeMap for latest-only search; assuming cancellation guarantees the server stops work; nesting subscriptions instead of composing streams.
followUps: switchMap vs concatMap?
What if the request is not cancellable server-side?
How would you debounce input?

questions.question: What is the difference between reactive forms and template-driven forms?
questions.shortAnswer: Reactive forms define form state and validation in TypeScript, while template-driven forms rely more on directives and template configuration. Reactive forms are usually easier to scale and test for complex forms.
questions.detailedAnswer: The choice depends on complexity. Simple forms can be readable with template-driven APIs; large forms benefit from explicit reactive state and validators.
questions.example: A multi-step customer onboarding form with conditional fields, cross-field validation and dynamic controls is easier to model with FormGroup and FormControl.
questions.seniorPerspective: For enterprise forms I value explicit validation, testability and predictable state transitions.
questions.commonMistakes: Putting complex validation logic into templates; duplicating validation between client and server; forgetting server-side validation.
followUps: How do you implement cross-field validation?
How do you handle dynamic FormArray controls?
Why is server validation still required?

questions.question: What are Angular signals and when would you use them?
questions.shortAnswer: Signals represent reactive state that Angular can track directly. They are useful for local UI state and derived values, while RxJS remains strong for asynchronous streams and event composition.
questions.detailedAnswer: Signals simplify synchronous reactive state. I would not replace every Observable with a signal; the correct abstraction depends on whether the problem is state derivation or asynchronous stream composition.
questions.example: A product list can hold the selected filter in a signal and derive a filtered count with computed. An HTTP stream can still use RxJS and then update signal-based view state.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose signals for clear local reactive state and RxJS where stream operators, cancellation and async composition matter.
questions.commonMistakes: Using effects for ordinary derived state; converting every Observable to a signal without understanding lifecycle; creating hidden side effects.
followUps: Signal vs BehaviorSubject?
What is computed used for?
When would you keep RxJS?

questions.question: How does the JavaScript event loop work?
questions.shortAnswer: JavaScript runs synchronous code on a call stack and uses queues for asynchronous callbacks. Microtasks such as Promise continuations are processed before the next macrotask such as a timer callback.
questions.detailedAnswer: The event loop does not make CPU-heavy JavaScript non-blocking. A long synchronous loop can still freeze the browser even while asynchronous APIs exist.
questions.example: If a UI handler schedules a Promise callback and setTimeout, the Promise continuation normally runs first after the current synchronous stack completes. Understanding this helps explain ordering bugs.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use the event loop model to reason about ordering, responsiveness and race conditions.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying async code always runs in parallel; ignoring microtask ordering; using setTimeout as a reliable synchronization primitive.
followUps: Promise vs setTimeout ordering?
Why can a browser freeze despite async APIs?
How would you move CPU-heavy work?

questions.question: What is the difference between interface and type in TypeScript?
questions.shortAnswer: Both can describe shapes, but interfaces are designed for object contracts and declaration merging, while type aliases are more flexible for unions, intersections and computed types.
questions.detailedAnswer: The practical difference is expressiveness and API intent rather than a rule that one is always better. Consistency across a codebase matters.
questions.example: A public domain model such as Customer can be an interface. A Result type such as Success<T> | Failure can be a type alias because a union is required.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use the construct that best communicates whether I am defining an extensible object contract or a more general type expression.
questions.commonMistakes: Treating interface and type as completely interchangeable; ignoring declaration merging; choosing based only on personal preference in a shared codebase.
followUps: Can interfaces represent unions?
What is declaration merging?
How would you model API success and error results?

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.shortAnswer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
questions.detailedAnswer: Filtering early with WHERE can reduce rows that reach aggregation. HAVING is for conditions on grouped or aggregated results.
questions.example: To find customers whose total order value exceeds 10000, WHERE can restrict orders by date first, GROUP BY CustomerId calculates totals, and HAVING filters totals above 10000.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use the clause that matches the stage of the relational operation and check the execution plan for expensive scans or sorts.
questions.commonMistakes: Using HAVING for ordinary row filters; forgetting grouped columns; assuming SQL evaluates clauses in the textual order they appear.
followUps: Can WHERE use an aggregate?
How would you filter before grouping for performance?
How does GROUP BY affect row count?

questions.question: What is a deadlock and how do you reduce deadlocks in SQL Server?
questions.shortAnswer: A deadlock occurs when transactions hold locks that each needs the other to release. SQL Server chooses a victim and rolls it back.
questions.detailedAnswer: Other tools include appropriate indexes, smaller batches, suitable isolation levels and retrying a known transient deadlock where the operation is safe to retry.
questions.example: If transaction A updates Account then Ledger while transaction B updates Ledger then Account, they can wait on each other. Consistent lock ordering and shorter transactions reduce the risk.
questions.seniorPerspective: I investigate the deadlock graph rather than adding blind retries.
questions.commonMistakes: Catching every deadlock and retrying indefinitely; ignoring transaction order; keeping transactions open during network calls.
followUps: How do you capture a deadlock graph?
Why can indexes reduce deadlocks?
When is retry safe?

questions.question: What is parameter sniffing in SQL Server?
questions.shortAnswer: Parameter sniffing occurs when SQL Server compiles a plan using one parameter's characteristics and later reuses that plan for values with very different data distributions.
questions.detailedAnswer: I confirm the issue with execution plans, statistics and parameter-specific behavior before choosing a mitigation such as query rewriting, recompilation or plan management.
questions.example: A query filtering Orders by CustomerId may be fast for a customer with 20 rows but poor for a customer with millions. A cached plan optimized for one distribution can perform badly for another.
questions.seniorPerspective: The senior response is evidence-driven: identify the plan problem, understand data skew, then choose the least risky mitigation.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding OPTION(RECOMPILE) everywhere; blaming parameter sniffing without comparing plans; ignoring stale statistics.
followUps: How would you prove parameter sniffing?
What are the trade-offs of recompilation?
How do statistics affect plans?

questions.question: How would you design a URL shortening service?
questions.shortAnswer: I would store a unique short code mapped to the original URL, expose create and redirect APIs, and consider caching, expiration, abuse prevention and analytics separately from the core mapping.
questions.detailedAnswer: At higher scale, read traffic dominates, so caching and partitioning may matter. Analytics should not make redirects depend on a slow synchronous write path.
questions.example: Creating a short URL writes the mapping to a database. Redirect requests first check a cache and fall back to the database. The code can be generated from a sequence, random ID or encoded identifier with collision handling.
questions.seniorPerspective: I would state expected traffic, URL lifetime, consistency needs and abuse requirements before choosing storage and caching details.
questions.commonMistakes: Choosing a database without estimating read/write patterns; making analytics synchronous; ignoring malicious URLs and rate limits.
followUps: How would you generate collision-free IDs?
How would you scale redirects?
What happens if cache and database disagree?

questions.question: What is an IDOR vulnerability and how do you prevent it?
questions.shortAnswer: Insecure direct object reference occurs when a user can access another user's resource by changing an identifier because the server checks authentication but not ownership or permission.
questions.detailedAnswer: Authorization should be enforced server-side and ideally close to the resource query. Negative tests should prove that cross-user and cross-tenant access is denied.
questions.example: GET /orders/1001 is requested by user A, who changes the ID to 1002 belonging to user B. The server must derive the caller identity from trusted authentication and enforce ownership or permission in the data access path.
questions.seniorPerspective: I treat resource authorization as part of the endpoint's contract, not an optional UI check.
questions.commonMistakes: Relying on hidden IDs; checking only whether the user is logged in; implementing authorization in Angular guards alone.
followUps: How would you test for IDOR?
How does multi-tenancy change the check?
Why is obscurity not authorization?

questions.question: How does garbage collection work in .NET and how can a memory leak still occur?
questions.shortAnswer: The GC reclaims objects that are no longer reachable. A managed application can still leak memory when live references are retained unintentionally, such as event subscriptions, static collections or caches without eviction.
questions.detailedAnswer: I inspect heap snapshots, allocation patterns and object retention paths. The fix is usually ownership and lifecycle, not calling GC manually.
questions.example: A singleton cache stores every request payload keyed by ID and never removes old entries. The objects remain reachable, so GC cannot reclaim them. Memory grows even though there is no unmanaged allocation.
questions.seniorPerspective: The senior distinction is between allocation pressure, fragmentation and true retention. I change code based on profiling evidence.
questions.commonMistakes: Calling GC.Collect as a normal fix; assuming managed memory cannot leak; optimizing allocations before finding retained roots.
followUps: How do you diagnose a managed memory leak?
What is LOH?
How can a cache create retention?

questions.question: How would you diagnose ThreadPool starvation in an ASP.NET Core application?
questions.shortAnswer: I would look for blocked ThreadPool threads, slow request latency, synchronous I/O, excessive work and queue growth. The fix is usually removing blocking or reducing work rather than simply increasing threads.
questions.detailedAnswer: I would correlate ThreadPool metrics, request latency, dependency timings and traces, then reproduce under load. Async I/O and bounded concurrency usually address the root cause.
questions.example: An endpoint calls a synchronous database API and blocks many request threads while SQL is slow. Under load, available worker threads become scarce and unrelated requests wait, causing latency to spike.
questions.seniorPerspective: Senior diagnosis connects runtime symptoms to the blocking dependency and validates the fix with a representative load test.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding threads blindly; converting everything to Task.Run; measuring only average latency; ignoring downstream saturation.
followUps: What causes ThreadPool starvation?
Why does async I/O help?
How would you prove the fix?

questions.question: How would you design an idempotent API operation?
questions.shortAnswer: An idempotent operation produces the same business outcome when the same request is retried. I use an idempotency key or a naturally unique business key and persist the outcome so duplicate requests do not repeat the side effect.
questions.detailedAnswer: Idempotency needs a durable uniqueness boundary, clear key scope and handling for concurrent duplicate requests. It is especially important when clients retry after timeouts.
questions.example: A payment client times out after the server processes the payment. The client retries with the same idempotency key. The server finds the existing key and returns the original result instead of charging again.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design idempotency around the business invariant, not just around HTTP method names.
questions.commonMistakes: Generating a key only in memory; making the idempotency record expire too quickly; returning success before the durable side effect is safe.
followUps: Where should the idempotency key be stored?
How do you handle concurrent retries?
Can an HTTP POST be idempotent?

questions.question: How would you design a high-throughput ASP.NET Core API?
questions.shortAnswer: I would first define throughput and latency targets, then keep the request path efficient: async I/O, efficient database queries, appropriate caching, bounded concurrency, small payloads and observability.
questions.detailedAnswer: High throughput is a system property. Optimizing application code while SQL is saturated or a downstream API is slow will not solve the actual constraint.
questions.example: For a read-heavy catalog API, I would project only required columns, index the access pattern, cache stable data and use async database calls. Load tests would identify whether the bottleneck is CPU, database, network or downstream services.
questions.seniorPerspective: I optimize the dominant bottleneck and protect dependencies with timeouts, rate limits and bounded concurrency.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding cache everywhere; increasing server count while the database is the bottleneck; ignoring tail latency and error rate.
followUps: How do you find the bottleneck?
What would you cache?
How would you protect a slow downstream service?

questions.question: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic concurrency?
questions.shortAnswer: Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are uncommon and detects them at update time, often with a row version. Pessimistic concurrency prevents conflicting changes by locking earlier.
questions.detailedAnswer: Optimistic concurrency usually scales better for many read-heavy workflows because it avoids long locks, but conflict handling must be designed. Pessimistic locking can be appropriate for short critical sections with high contention.
questions.example: An admin edits a customer record while another process updates it. With a rowversion column, the second update can detect that the version changed and return a concurrency conflict instead of silently overwriting data.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose based on contention, business impact of conflicts and transaction duration.
questions.commonMistakes: Using last-write-wins for data where overwrites are unacceptable; holding locks across slow operations; retrying conflicts without understanding business semantics.
followUps: How does EF Core implement optimistic concurrency?
When would pessimistic locking be justified?
How should a UI handle a conflict?

questions.question: How would you improve performance in a large Angular application?
questions.shortAnswer: I would measure first, then reduce unnecessary rendering and network work using lazy loading, OnPush or signals, trackBy, smaller bundles, efficient RxJS flows and appropriate caching.
questions.detailedAnswer: Performance is a combination of bundle size, network, change detection, DOM size and API latency. A frontend optimization that increases stale data or complexity may not be worth it.
questions.example: A large admin application can lazy-load rarely used areas, use OnPush components, avoid calling expensive methods from templates, virtualize long lists and cache stable lookup data.
questions.seniorPerspective: I use browser profiling and production telemetry to identify the largest contributor before changing architecture.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding OnPush everywhere without understanding state updates; optimizing CSS while API latency dominates; rendering thousands of DOM nodes.
followUps: How would you profile Angular rendering?
When is virtualization useful?
How would you reduce initial bundle size?

questions.question: How would you prevent stale HTTP results and race conditions in an Angular application?
questions.shortAnswer: I model the request flow explicitly: switchMap for latest-only searches, cancellation for obsolete requests, request identifiers when ordering matters, and state updates that verify the response still belongs to the current operation.
questions.detailedAnswer: Cancellation on the client does not guarantee the server stops work, so backend operations still need timeouts and cancellation. For mutations, blindly cancelling can be dangerous.
questions.example: A user changes filters quickly from A to B. Request A returns after B and would overwrite the UI. A switchMap-based stream makes the latest filter authoritative.
questions.seniorPerspective: I distinguish latest-only reads from mutations that must complete, then choose the RxJS operator and backend behavior accordingly.
questions.commonMistakes: Using switchMap for non-idempotent mutations; assuming browser cancellation guarantees server cancellation; storing request state in multiple unrelated subscriptions.
followUps: switchMap vs concatMap?
How do you handle retries?
How would you make a mutation safe to retry?

questions.question: How would you troubleshoot a query that suddenly became slow in production?
questions.shortAnswer: I would compare current and previous execution plans, runtime statistics, row counts, blocking, waits, parameter values, statistics and recent schema or data changes before changing the query.
questions.detailedAnswer: The same symptom can have different causes: plan regression, blocking, IO pressure, stale statistics, parameter sensitivity or infrastructure contention. Evidence determines the fix.
questions.example: An order search that normally runs in 100 ms starts taking 8 seconds. I would check whether the plan changed, whether a new data distribution caused a bad plan, whether blocking exists, and whether the query now scans a large table.
questions.seniorPerspective: I preserve the ability to compare the incident with a known-good period and validate the fix under representative parameters.
questions.commonMistakes: Rebuilding indexes blindly; adding NOLOCK without understanding correctness; assuming a slow query is always an index problem.
followUps: How do you identify blocking?
How do you compare execution plans?
What if the query is fast alone but slow under load?

questions.question: How do transaction isolation levels affect correctness and concurrency?
questions.shortAnswer: Isolation controls which effects of concurrent transactions are visible. Higher isolation can provide stronger consistency but may increase locking or version-store usage depending on the implementation.
questions.detailedAnswer: I choose isolation based on the business anomaly that must be prevented, not by choosing the strongest level by default.
questions.example: A reporting query running under a strong isolation level can hold or interact with locks long enough to affect OLTP traffic. Row-versioning options can change that behavior, but they have storage and workload implications.
questions.seniorPerspective: I explicitly identify whether dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom rows or lost updates matter to the operation.
questions.commonMistakes: Using NOLOCK to hide blocking; assuming Serializable is always safest; ignoring version-store and write contention.
followUps: Which anomalies does each isolation level address?
When is snapshot useful?
How would you prevent lost updates?

questions.question: How would you paginate millions of rows efficiently?
questions.shortAnswer: For large ordered datasets, keyset or seek pagination is often better than large OFFSET values because the database can continue from the last key instead of scanning and discarding many rows.
questions.detailedAnswer: Offset pagination is convenient for random page numbers but can become expensive and unstable when data changes. Keyset requires a stable ordering and cursor representation.
questions.example: An export or activity feed ordered by CreatedAt and Id can return the next page using WHERE (CreatedAt,Id) is after the last cursor, with a matching index.
questions.seniorPerspective: I choose pagination based on navigation requirements, consistency and scale, then validate the query plan.
questions.commonMistakes: Using OFFSET for deep pages without measuring; ordering by a non-unique column; exposing raw database keys as cursors without considering API stability.
followUps: How do you handle duplicate timestamps?
What index supports keyset pagination?
When is OFFSET acceptable?

questions.question: How would you design a notification system that supports email, SMS and push?
questions.shortAnswer: I would separate notification intent from delivery. A producer records the notification request, a queue buffers work, channel-specific workers deliver it, and status is persisted for retries and audit.
questions.detailedAnswer: The design needs backpressure, retry classification, provider rate limits, idempotency, observability and user preferences. Synchronous delivery would couple order completion to provider availability.
questions.example: An order service publishes OrderShipped. A notification service creates email and push jobs. Workers consume them with provider-specific retry policies and idempotency keys. A dead-letter path captures persistent failures.
questions.seniorPerspective: I keep the business transaction independent from slow external notification providers.
questions.commonMistakes: Retrying permanent failures forever; publishing events without durable ownership; no idempotency; making notification delivery block the core transaction.
followUps: How do you guarantee delivery?
How do you handle duplicate messages?
How would you scale workers?

questions.question: How would you design a distributed rate limiter?
questions.shortAnswer: I would define the limit, identity and time window first, then choose a shared counter or token-bucket mechanism with atomic updates and an explicit failure policy.
questions.detailedAnswer: Distributed rate limiting introduces network latency and dependency failure. Local limits can protect an instance, while a shared limiter provides a more consistent global policy.
questions.example: An API gateway can use a Redis-backed token bucket keyed by API key. Atomic operations ensure concurrent instances cannot all accept requests based on stale local counters.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design both the normal path and the behavior when the limiter store is unavailable.
questions.commonMistakes: Using process-local counters for a global limit; non-atomic read-modify-write; forgetting burst behavior; failing open without assessing abuse risk.
followUps: Fixed window vs token bucket?
What happens if Redis is unavailable?
How do you avoid hot keys?

questions.question: How would you design a scalable order-processing system?
questions.shortAnswer: I would keep the order state and critical invariants in a transactional store, then use durable events or queues for asynchronous work such as payment workflows, inventory updates and notifications.
questions.detailedAnswer: The outbox pattern helps avoid the dual-write problem. Consumers need idempotency because at-least-once delivery can produce duplicates.
questions.example: Order creation writes an order and an outbox event in one transaction. A worker publishes the event and downstream consumers process it idempotently. State transitions are explicit so retries do not duplicate business effects.
questions.seniorPerspective: I design around business state transitions and failure recovery rather than assuming distributed transactions are available.
questions.commonMistakes: Assuming exactly-once delivery; updating multiple systems without an outbox or equivalent; unclear state transitions; no reconciliation process.
followUps: Why use an outbox?
How do you handle duplicate events?
What if payment succeeds but the order service times out?

questions.question: How would you secure a public REST API?
questions.shortAnswer: I would combine strong authentication, authorization, input validation, TLS, rate limiting, safe error handling, secret management, audit logging and dependency security. The exact controls depend on the threat model.
questions.detailedAnswer: Security is layered because any single control can fail. I also protect dependencies and operational surfaces such as logs, CI/CD and administrative endpoints.
questions.example: A public customer API validates JWTs, checks resource ownership, limits abusive clients, validates payloads, stores secrets in a secret manager and records security-relevant actions. Sensitive endpoints receive tighter controls.
questions.seniorPerspective: I threat-model the assets and trust boundaries first, then make important controls testable in CI and production monitoring.
questions.commonMistakes: Relying on authentication alone; putting secrets in source control; logging tokens or passwords; trusting client-provided tenant IDs.
followUps: How do you prevent replay?
How would you protect file upload endpoints?
What security tests belong in CI?

questions.question: How would you implement secure JWT refresh-token handling?
questions.shortAnswer: I would use short-lived access tokens and securely managed refresh tokens, rotate refresh tokens where appropriate, detect reuse, validate audience and issuer, and revoke compromised sessions.
questions.detailedAnswer: Token storage and browser architecture matter. I would minimize token exposure, define revocation behavior and handle concurrent refresh requests so multiple tabs do not create inconsistent sessions.
questions.example: A browser application uses an access token for API calls and a refresh token mechanism to obtain a new access token. When a refresh token is used, the server rotates it and invalidates the previous token so replay can be detected.
questions.seniorPerspective: I treat refresh as a security-sensitive state machine, not just another API endpoint.
questions.commonMistakes: Long-lived access tokens; no refresh-token rotation or reuse detection; exposing tokens unnecessarily; ignoring concurrent refresh races.
followUps: How do you revoke tokens?
What happens if a refresh token is stolen?
How do you coordinate refresh across browser tabs?

questions.question: How would you investigate an intermittent production issue that cannot be reproduced locally?
questions.shortAnswer: I would improve correlation first: request ID, user or business identifier where safe, structured logs, traces, dependency timings and environment information. Then compare successful and failed requests.
questions.detailedAnswer: The goal is to reduce uncertainty before changing code. Reproduction may require production-like load, data or timing, so observability is often the first engineering fix.
questions.example: If 1% of checkout requests fail, I would group failures by version, region, dependency, input shape and timing. A trace might show that only requests routed to one downstream instance exceed a timeout.
questions.seniorPerspective: I preserve evidence, mitigate user impact, then move from symptom to root cause and add a regression test or monitoring signal.
questions.commonMistakes: Guessing from one stack trace; adding unlimited logging; changing several things before collecting evidence; ignoring data privacy in diagnostics.
followUps: What telemetry would you add?
How would you compare failed and successful traces?
How do you prevent the diagnostic change from adding load?

questions.question: How would you decide whether to rollback a production release?
questions.shortAnswer: I would consider severity, user impact, correlation with the release, confidence in the mitigation, rollback safety and whether the previous version is known-good.
questions.detailedAnswer: Rollback is mitigation, not proof of root cause. I preserve logs, metrics and deployment metadata so the later investigation can establish why the regression occurred.
questions.example: If error rate and latency rise immediately after a release and the previous version is healthy, rollback can restore service while the investigation continues. Database changes require extra care because application rollback may not be compatible with schema changes.
questions.seniorPerspective: A senior engineer optimizes for safe service restoration while keeping the incident evidence intact.
questions.commonMistakes: Rolling back automatically without considering irreversible migrations; treating rollback as root-cause analysis; failing to communicate impact and next steps.
followUps: When would you roll forward instead?
How do backward-compatible migrations help?
What evidence should be preserved?

questions.question: How would you evaluate an enterprise RAG system?
questions.shortAnswer: I would evaluate retrieval and generation separately using representative questions and expected evidence. Metrics should cover retrieval relevance, answer correctness, citation quality, latency, cost and refusal behavior.
questions.detailedAnswer: Evaluation must include unanswerable questions, access-control cases and adversarial inputs. Production feedback should be sampled and monitored rather than relying on a one-time demo.
questions.example: For a support assistant, create a test set of real questions with approved source documents. Measure whether the correct document appears in the top results and whether the generated answer is supported by those sources.
questions.seniorPerspective: I want measurable release gates so a model or embedding change cannot silently degrade the workflow.
questions.commonMistakes: Evaluating only fluent answers; ignoring retrieval misses; allowing unauthorized documents into context; measuring model confidence as correctness.
followUps: How do you evaluate hallucination?
What if retrieval returns nothing?
How would you test access control?

questions.question: What is the difference between latency, throughput and resource utilization?
questions.shortAnswer: Latency is the time for one operation, throughput is how much work the system completes per unit time, and utilization describes how heavily resources such as CPU, memory or database connections are used.
questions.detailedAnswer: These metrics describe different failure modes. A system can be low-latency at low traffic and collapse under load because utilization approaches a saturation point.
questions.example: An API can have good average latency but poor throughput if every request consumes too much CPU. A reporting job may have high throughput while deliberately using more CPU during an off-peak window.
questions.seniorPerspective: I always name the metric before proposing an optimization.
questions.commonMistakes: Optimizing average latency while p95 is poor; confusing throughput with latency; ignoring saturation.
followUps: Why is p95 useful?
What happens near resource saturation?
Which metric would you monitor for an API?

questions.question: Why is measuring performance before optimization important?
questions.shortAnswer: Without a baseline, it is difficult to know whether a change helped, hurt another metric or simply moved the bottleneck.
questions.detailedAnswer: A good baseline includes representative traffic, p95 or p99 latency, error rate and resource usage. The same workload should be used after the change.
questions.example: If an API takes 900 ms, profiling may show 700 ms is SQL time. Rewriting a C# loop that costs 5 ms is unlikely to produce a meaningful improvement.
questions.seniorPerspective: Senior optimization is evidence-driven rather than based on code that merely looks slow.
questions.commonMistakes: Optimizing the most visible code instead of the dominant cost; using only local benchmarks; ignoring tail latency.
followUps: How do you choose a representative workload?
Which percentile would you track?
How do you validate a performance fix?

questions.question: How does caching improve performance and what problems can it introduce?
questions.shortAnswer: Caching avoids repeated expensive work by reusing data, but it introduces freshness, invalidation, memory and consistency concerns.
questions.detailedAnswer: I define what can be stale, how long it can be stale, how invalidation happens and what occurs when the cache is unavailable.
questions.example: A product catalog that changes every few minutes can be cached for a short TTL. A customer's current account balance should not be served from a stale cache without a business rule allowing that behavior.
questions.seniorPerspective: The senior decision is whether the consistency trade-off is acceptable for the business operation.
questions.commonMistakes: Caching highly dynamic data; no eviction policy; cache stampede; treating cache as the source of truth.
followUps: What is cache-aside?
How do you prevent stampedes?
What happens when the cache is unavailable?

questions.question: What is connection pooling and why does it matter for database performance?
questions.shortAnswer: Connection pooling reuses database connections instead of establishing a new physical connection for every operation. It reduces connection setup overhead but the pool is still a finite resource.
questions.detailedAnswer: A pool that is exhausted can cause requests to wait. Long-running queries and leaked connections can therefore look like application latency problems.
questions.example: If an API opens a new database connection for every request and traffic spikes, connection creation and database authentication can become expensive. Pooling reuses connections while limiting concurrency.
questions.seniorPerspective: I monitor pool waits together with SQL duration and request latency.
questions.commonMistakes: Opening connections and never disposing them; increasing pool size without checking database capacity; confusing pooled connections with unlimited connections.
followUps: What causes pool exhaustion?
How does async disposal help?
Should pool size always be increased?

questions.question: How would you investigate high API p99 latency when average latency looks normal?
questions.shortAnswer: I would segment requests by endpoint, dependency, instance, region and request characteristics and inspect traces and percentile distributions rather than relying on the average.
questions.detailedAnswer: Tail latency often comes from contention, retries, queueing or outliers. The fix should target the source of the long tail rather than making the average path faster.
questions.example: If average latency is 150 ms but p99 is 5 seconds, a small fraction of requests may be hitting a slow SQL plan, lock wait or downstream timeout. Distributed tracing can show where those tail requests spend time.
questions.seniorPerspective: I would compare p50, p95 and p99 before and after the change and verify error rates did not increase.
questions.commonMistakes: Optimizing only the median; increasing timeouts to hide slow dependencies; ignoring retry amplification.
followUps: How do retries affect p99?
How would you identify the slow dependency?
When should a timeout be reduced?

questions.question: What is backpressure and why is it important in distributed systems?
questions.shortAnswer: Backpressure prevents producers from overwhelming consumers by bounding queues, concurrency or ingestion rates.
questions.detailedAnswer: Backpressure protects system stability. The product decision is whether to queue, throttle, reject or degrade when demand exceeds sustainable capacity.
questions.example: If an API accepts files faster than a worker can process them, an unbounded queue grows until memory or storage is exhausted. A bounded queue can slow or reject producers when capacity is reached.
questions.seniorPerspective: I define capacity limits and observable overload behavior rather than allowing queues to grow without bounds.
questions.commonMistakes: Unbounded queues; unlimited worker concurrency; retry storms during overload; no user-visible overload policy.
followUps: How do you implement bounded concurrency?
What metrics show overload?
When should an API return 429?

questions.question: How would you answer 'Tell me about yourself' for a 7-year software engineer interview?
questions.shortAnswer: I would give a concise career summary, current technical strengths, the kinds of systems I have worked on, and what I am looking for next. I would keep it relevant to the role rather than narrating every job.
questions.detailedAnswer: The senior signal is progression: increasing scope, judgment, ownership and impact. The answer should create clear threads for the interviewer to explore.
questions.example: A strong two-minute answer can cover progression from implementation to owning features, debugging production issues, making design decisions and collaborating across teams, followed by the technologies most relevant to the job.
questions.seniorPerspective: I prepare a flexible version that can be tailored to backend, full-stack or platform roles without memorizing a script.
questions.commonMistakes: Listing every technology; reading the resume aloud; giving personal history unrelated to the role; making unsupported claims.
followUps: How has your role changed over seven years?
What are your strongest technical areas?
What kind of role are you targeting?

questions.question: Tell me about a technical disagreement you had with a teammate. How did you handle it?
questions.shortAnswer: I would explain the decision, the evidence behind my position, the other person's concern, how we tested or compared the options, and the final outcome. I would avoid framing the story as proving someone wrong.
questions.detailedAnswer: Senior behavior is evidence-based influence: understand the other constraint, make the disagreement concrete, and keep the relationship separate from the technical decision.
questions.example: For a debate about caching versus fixing a slow query, I could profile the endpoint, show that an index removed most of the latency, agree to revisit caching after measuring production behavior, and document the decision.
questions.seniorPerspective: I focus on what I personally did and what I learned, not on blaming the other engineer.
questions.commonMistakes: Saying the other person was wrong; giving no action of your own; ending with 'we agreed' without explaining why.
followUps: What would you do if they still disagreed?
Did you change your mind?
What did you learn?

questions.question: Tell me about a production failure you were responsible for. What did you learn?
questions.shortAnswer: I would own the part I controlled, explain how I mitigated the impact, identify the root cause, and describe the process or technical change that prevents recurrence.
questions.detailedAnswer: A senior answer demonstrates accountability without pretending one person caused every system failure. The learning should change future engineering behavior.
questions.example: If a release caused an unexpected error spike, I would explain the rollback or mitigation, the evidence that identified the change, the missing test or guardrail, and the follow-up monitoring or deployment improvement.
questions.seniorPerspective: I would quantify impact where possible and be ready for detailed follow-up about what I would do differently.
questions.commonMistakes: Blaming another team; presenting a failure with no personal contribution; claiming 'we added tests' without explaining what test or why it closes the gap.
followUps: What was the root cause?
What would you do differently?
How did you verify the fix?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you influenced a technical decision without having authority.
questions.shortAnswer: I would describe the decision, stakeholders, constraints, evidence I gathered, how I communicated it and the outcome. Influence should come from clarity and trust rather than title.
questions.detailedAnswer: At seven years, the interviewer is often looking for influence across boundaries: making decisions clearer for others and accepting the team's final decision once the evidence is considered.
questions.example: For a proposed architecture change, I could compare operational cost, migration risk and delivery time, run a small proof of concept, and use the evidence in a design review so the team could choose an incremental approach.
questions.seniorPerspective: I would distinguish influencing a decision from forcing my preferred solution.
questions.commonMistakes: Claiming the team followed because of seniority; focusing on meetings rather than decisions; ignoring legitimate opposing constraints.
followUps: What if your recommendation was rejected?
How did you build alignment?
What did you learn from the final decision?

questions.question: How do you handle ambiguous requirements as a senior developer?
questions.shortAnswer: I turn ambiguity into explicit assumptions, identify the highest-risk unknowns, confirm the business outcome, and propose a small implementation that can validate the direction before large investment.
questions.detailedAnswer: Senior engineers reduce ambiguity for the team. The goal is not to wait for a perfect specification but to make uncertainty visible and manageable.
questions.example: If a product request says 'make the dashboard faster,' I would clarify the user journey and target metric, measure current latency, identify the bottleneck and agree on a measurable acceptance criterion before redesigning the system.
questions.seniorPerspective: I document decisions and assumptions so later changes can be made intentionally rather than rediscovering why the design exists.
questions.commonMistakes: Starting implementation with hidden assumptions; asking endless clarification questions; solving the wrong problem efficiently.
followUps: How do you proceed if the stakeholder is unavailable?
What assumptions would you document?
When would you stop and escalate?

questions.question: Tell me about a time you mentored or enabled another engineer.
questions.shortAnswer: I would focus on how I helped the person become more independent, not just on the task I completed for them.
questions.detailedAnswer: Senior impact includes multiplying team capability. The strongest example shows a repeatable practice such as design reviews, debugging walkthroughs or documentation.
questions.example: For a developer struggling with a production issue, I could guide them through log correlation, hypothesis formation and validation, then let them implement the fix while I reviewed the approach. A useful outcome is that they handled a similar issue independently later.
questions.seniorPerspective: I explain the coaching choice and the measurable or observable improvement in the person's independence.
questions.commonMistakes: Taking over the task; teaching only through theory; presenting another engineer's success as my own.
followUps: How did you adapt your mentoring style?
What did the engineer do independently later?
What would you improve about your approach?

questions.question: What is the difference between an AI agent and a normal LLM call?
questions.shortAnswer: A normal LLM call produces an answer from a prompt. An agentic workflow can plan or select actions, call tools, inspect results and continue toward a goal under defined constraints.
questions.detailedAnswer: Agentic behavior increases capability and risk. Reliability comes from deterministic tool boundaries, authorization, timeouts, budgets and auditability around the model.
questions.example: A support assistant can retrieve an issue, search approved documentation, analyze logs and draft a proposed fix. Each tool call should have explicit permissions and structured inputs rather than giving the model unrestricted system access.
questions.seniorPerspective: I separate probabilistic reasoning from deterministic business controls.
questions.commonMistakes: Giving an agent unrestricted tools; no timeout or cost budget; trusting model-generated parameters without validation.
followUps: How do you secure tools?
How do you stop infinite loops?
When is a simple LLM call better?

questions.question: How would you reduce hallucinations in an enterprise AI assistant?
questions.shortAnswer: I would improve retrieval quality, constrain the answer to approved context, require citations where appropriate, allow explicit 'I don't know' behavior and evaluate against representative questions.
questions.detailedAnswer: Hallucination reduction is a system problem, not just a prompt problem. Retrieval, authorization, model choice, output validation and evaluation all contribute.
questions.example: For an internal support assistant, retrieve only documents the user can access, include source metadata, instruct the model to answer only from supplied evidence, and return no-answer when retrieval confidence is insufficient.
questions.seniorPerspective: I would measure unsupported-answer rate and retrieval misses separately.
questions.commonMistakes: Adding a stronger prompt without measuring retrieval; exposing private documents; forcing an answer when evidence is missing.
followUps: How do you detect unsupported claims?
What if two sources conflict?
How do you evaluate a no-answer policy?
